newsitem.title: ITALY: GLACIER BALANCING ABOVE ITALIAN SKI RESORT.
newsitem.headline: GLACIER BALANCING ABOVE ITALIAN SKI RESORT.

text.p: The first chunk of a huge hanging glacier threatening a hamlet near the Italian ski resort of Courmayeur has broken off and hopes are growing the ice may not cause much damage, Courmayeur's mayor said on Friday.
Ferdinando Derriard said around 100 cubic metres of ice had broken off the nose of the glacier on the Grandes Jorasses peaks on the Mont Blanc massif in northwestern Italy.
"A small bit has broken off. There's still the main part which has to break off," Derriard told Reuters by telephone. "It's there balancing. We're waiting for it to fall."

Experts say a lump of ice about 70 metres (230 feet) high, 100 metres (330 feet) across and two or three metres (seven to 10 feet) deep is poised to detach itself at any moment from the body of the glacier as it moves forward.
Oscar Taiola, head of Courmayeur's avalanche committee, said by telephone the piece had broken off during Wednesday night.

"A small bit on the right hand side has dropped and it's a sign there's movement. But it's all still, all the same as yesterday. We don't know (when it will fall), between today and tomorrow certainly, or maybe the day after tomorrow -- but it's imminent," he said.
The glacier is 12 km (7.5 miles) from Courmayeur and its downhill pistes, which are in a different area of the valley, and authorities say the popular ski resort is not threatened.

But Planpincieux, a mountain hamlet in Val Ferret, the valley which an avalanche caused by the falling ice is expected to hit, has been evacuated, the road up to it closed and a cross country piste placed out of bounds.
Derriard said, however, that hopes were growing that the ice would fall off in pieces and so cause little damage.
The impact of the falling ice is hard to predict, with less damage coming from the initial chunk than the snow it pushes before it as it slides down the slope and forms an avalanche.
Above the valley, the sun was shining and Derriard said everything was visible including the path the detached piece of ice had taken.
Asked if it looked likely to fall in the path they had predicted, he said: "Yes, where it shouldn't cause damage."
